title: What Difficult Students Desperately Need, But Rarely Get t-rarely-get/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that what difficult students need most isn't more attention but honest feedback—an accurate, compassionate reflection of how they're actually doing. He describes how these students are typically caught between gratuitous praise for meeting baseline expectations and harsh personal criticism for mistakes, leaving them with a distorted picture of themselves. His proposed remedy leans on a fair, consistent classroom management plan as the primary 'unspoken truth,' supplemented occasionally by brief, plainly stated verbal truths delivered without lingering for a response. The piece closes by framing honest feedback as a gift that can pull students off the 'roller coaster' of false praise and criticism and onto solid ground.
points: Difficult students typically receive too much attention and too little honest feedback, leaving them with a distorted self-image.
They are commonly caught between gratuitous praise for baseline behavior and harsh personal criticism for mistakes—neither of which is accurate feedback.
A fair, consistent classroom management plan functions as the primary 'unspoken truth' that communicates accountability without personal judgment.
When direct verbal feedback is warranted, it should be brief, plainly stated, and delivered without lingering for a response ('That isn't good enough,' then walking away).
Saying nothing at all in response to good behavior is described as often the most powerful message that right behavior is simply expected.
quotes: No, it’s not attention. For the most part difficult students are given far too much attention.
No, what your most challenging students need most is your honest feedback.
Most difficult students are subjected to a baffling combination of false praise and angry criticism. Teachers volley between the two like Federer and Nadal.
The only way difficult students can begin climbing out of the hole they’ve dug themselves is to know how deep the hole is.

The unspoken truth is your fair and consistent classroom management plan. Its action-based accountability clearly communicates that their behavior has strayed from the habits necessary for success in school.
